section.title: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Statue
section.sectionRationale: The king dreams of a towering statue of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, smashed to dust by a stone cut without human hands, and no one in Babylon can recover or interpret it. God reveals the mystery to Daniel, who declares that a succession of empires will rise and fall, but the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that lasts forever. This is the theological spine of the whole book: earthly power is real but passing, and God's kingdom will fill the earth.
section.thesis: The God of heaven, who alone reveals mysteries and removes and raises kings, shows Nebuchadnezzar that every human empire, however golden, will crumble, while the everlasting kingdom cut from the mountain without human hands will shatter them all and fill the earth.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the king's troubling dream and impossible demand; Daniel seeks mercy and the mystery is revealed; Daniel recounts the statue; the four kingdoms and the stone that becomes a mountain; and Nebuchadnezzar honors Daniel and his God.

units.label: The troubling dream and impossible demand
units.note: tell me the dream and its meaning

verses.text: In the second year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams that troubled his spirit, and sleep escaped him.
So the king gave orders to summon the magicians, enchanters, sorcerers, and astrologers to explain his dreams. When they came and stood before the king,
he said to them, “I have had a dream, and my spirit is anxious to understand it.”
Then the astrologers answered the king in Aramaic, “O king, may you live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will give the interpretation.”
The king replied to the astrologers, “My word is final: If you do not tell me the dream and its interpretation, you will be cut into pieces and your houses will be reduced to rubble.
But if you tell me the dream and its interpretation, you will receive from me gifts and rewards and great honor. So tell me the dream and its interpretation.”
They answered a second time, “Let the king tell the dream to his servants, and we will give the interpretation.”
The king replied, “I know for sure that you are stalling for time because you see that my word is final.

If you do not tell me the dream, there is only one decree for you. You have conspired to speak before me false and fraudulent words, hoping the situation will change. Therefore tell me the dream, and I will know that you can give me its interpretation.”
The astrologers answered the king, “No one on earth can do what the king requests! No king, however great and powerful, has ever asked anything like this of any magician, enchanter, or astrologer.
What the king requests is so difficult that no one can tell it to him except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals.”
This response made the king so angry and furious that he gave orders to destroy all the wise men of Babylon.
So the decree went out that the wise men were to be executed, and men went to look for Daniel and his friends to execute them.

units.label: Daniel seeks mercy; the mystery revealed
units.note: he blessed the God of heaven

verses.text: When Arioch, the commander of the king's guard, went out to execute the wise men of Babylon, Daniel responded with discretion and tact.
“Why is the decree from the king so harsh?” he asked. Then Arioch explained the situation to Daniel.
So Daniel went in and asked the king to give him some time, so that he could give him the interpretation.
Then Daniel returned to his house and explained the matter to his friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,
urging them to plead for mercy from the {{elah_shemayya|God of heaven}} concerning this {{raz|mystery}}, so that Daniel and his friends would not be killed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
During the night, the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven
and declared: “Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, for wisdom and power belong to Him.
He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to the discerning.
He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him.

To You, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, because You have given me wisdom and power. And now You have made known to me what we have requested, for You have made known to us the dream of the king.”

units.label: Daniel recounts the statue
units.note: a God in heaven who reveals mysteries

verses.text: Therefore Daniel went to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon, and said to him, “Do not execute the wise men of Babylon! Bring me before the king, and I will give him the interpretation.”
Arioch hastily brought Daniel before the king and said to him, “I have found a man among the exiles from Judah who will tell the king the interpretation.”
The king responded to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, “Are you able to tell me what I saw in the dream, as well as its interpretation?”
Daniel answered the king, “No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires.

But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days. Your dream and the visions that came into your mind as you lay on your bed were these:
As you lay on your bed, O king, your thoughts turned to the future, and the Revealer of Mysteries made known to you what will happen.

And to me this mystery has been revealed, not because I have more wisdom than any man alive, but in order that the interpretation might be made known to the king, and that you may understand the thoughts of your mind.
As you, O king, were watching, a great statue appeared. A great and dazzling statue stood before you, and its form was awesome.
The head of the statue was pure gold, its chest and arms were silver, its belly and thighs were bronze,
its legs were iron, and its feet were part iron and part clay.
As you watched, a {{eben|stone}} was cut out, but not by human hands. It struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them.

Then the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold were shattered and became like chaff on the threshing floor in summer. The wind carried them away, and not a trace of them could be found. But the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

units.label: The four kingdoms and the everlasting stone
units.note: a kingdom that will never be destroyed

verses.text: This was the dream; now we will tell the king its interpretation.
You, O king, are the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given sovereignty, power, strength, and glory.
Wherever the sons of men or beasts of the field or birds of the air dwell, He has given them into your hand and has made you ruler over them all. You are that head of gold.
But after you, there will arise another kingdom, inferior to yours. Next, a third kingdom, one of bronze, will rule the whole earth.
Finally, there will be a fourth kingdom as strong as iron; for iron shatters and crushes all things, and like iron that crushes all things, it will shatter and crush all the others.

And just as you saw that the feet and toes were made partly of fired clay and partly of iron, so this will be a divided kingdom, yet some of the strength of iron will be in it, just as you saw the iron mixed with clay.
And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so this kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle.
As you saw the iron mixed with clay, so the peoples will mix with one another but will not hold together any more than iron mixes with clay.

In the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a {{malku|kingdom}} that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people. It will shatter all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but will itself stand forever.

And just as you saw a stone being cut out of the mountain without human hands, and it shattered the iron, bronze, clay, silver, and gold, so the great God has told the king what will happen in the future. The dream is true, and its interpretation is trustworthy.”

units.label: Nebuchadnezzar honors Daniel and his God
units.note: your God is the God of gods

verses.text: At this, King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face, paid homage to Daniel, and ordered that an offering and incense be presented to him.
The king said to Daniel, “Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery.”
Then the king promoted Daniel and gave him many generous gifts. He made him ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon.
And at Daniel's request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon, while Daniel remained in the king's court.

elah_shemayya.gloss: The God of heaven. A favorite title in Daniel and the exilic books, it confesses that the true God rules from heaven above every earthly throne. In a chapter about kingdoms that rise and fall, the phrase quietly settles the question of who is really in charge: not Babylon's gods, but the God of heaven.

raz.gloss: A mystery, a hidden secret. The word appears again and again in this chapter: the dream is a raz that no human wisdom can uncover, but the God of heaven reveals mysteries. In the New Testament the same idea of God's hidden plan now unveiled is taken up in the Greek word mystērion, applied to the gospel of Christ.

eben.gloss: A stone or rock. The stone is cut out without human hands, strikes the statue on its feet, and grows into a mountain that fills the earth. It stands for the kingdom God Himself sets up, not made by human effort; Scripture goes on to call Christ the stone the builders rejected who has become the cornerstone.

malku.gloss: Kingdom, kingship, reign. The word threads through the interpretation: kingdom after kingdom of gold, silver, bronze, and iron will rise and be shattered, but the malku the God of heaven sets up will never be destroyed and will stand forever. It is the everlasting kingdom that comes in Christ.

basic.context: Nebuchadnezzar has a dream that terrifies him and demands, impossibly, that his wise men tell him both the dream and its meaning or die. They cannot; only the gods could do this, they protest. Daniel asks for time, prays with his friends, and God reveals the mystery. Daniel tells the king he saw a great statue of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, struck and pulverized by a stone cut without human hands, a stone that then became a mountain filling the whole earth.
basic.hermeneutics: Daniel interprets the statue as a succession of world empires, each giving way to the next, and the stone as God's own everlasting kingdom that outlasts and overthrows them all. Christians agree on the main point, that God rules history and His kingdom will triumph, while differing on the precise identity of the four kingdoms. It is wise to hold the details with humility and the central message with confidence.
basic.originalLanguages: From verse 4 the book shifts into Aramaic, the language of the empire. The key words are elah shemayya, the God of heaven, who alone reveals the raz, the mystery, that no wise man can uncover; the eben, the stone cut without hands; and the malku, the kingdom that will never be destroyed.
basic.typology: The stone cut without human hands, which crushes the empires and grows to fill the earth, is a picture of God's kingdom that comes not by human power but by God's own act, fulfilled in Christ, the rejected stone who becomes the cornerstone and whose reign fills the world.
basic.christ: The everlasting kingdom set up by the God of heaven is the kingdom Jesus announces and brings. He is the stone the builders rejected, cut out not by human hands but by God, who breaks every proud power and whose reign will fill the whole earth and never end. The gospel is the mystery, once hidden, now revealed.
basic.god: God is the God of heaven who reveals mysteries, changes times and seasons, and removes and raises up kings. He is sovereign over the greatest empires, giving Nebuchadnezzar his power and able to take it away. History is not adrift; it is moving toward the everlasting kingdom God will establish.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 7 revisits the same four kingdoms as beasts. Psalm 2 shows God laughing at raging kings and installing His King. And in the Gospels, Jesus is the rejected stone, Matthew 21, whose kingdom, Mark 1, is at hand.
basic.oneStory: This dream lays out the whole shape of history: empire after empire, glittering and then gone, until the God of heaven sets up a kingdom that never ends. That kingdom arrives in Jesus, the stone cut without hands, and the whole Bible presses toward the day when it fills the earth and every rival power is blown away like chaff.

context.literary:
Daniel 2 is the first of the Aramaic chapters, and its first Aramaic words are the astrologers' reply in verse 4, as though the book changes tongue exactly where Babylon begins to speak. Chapters 2 to 7 then form a ring. The vision of four kingdoms in chapter 2 matches the vision of four beasts in chapter 7. The furnace of chapter 3 matches the lions' den of chapter 6, each a story of faithful servants condemned by royal decree and rescued. The two chapters in the middle, 4 and 5, are twin tales of a proud king humbled. Chapter 2 is therefore the outer edge of a structure whose centre is the humbling of Babylon's kings.

Within the chapter the scenes alternate between the court and the room where Daniel prays. The king's demand and the astrologers' protest fill verses 1 to 13; Daniel's tact and the night prayer of verses 14 to 23; the exchange with the king and the dream itself, verses 24 to 35; the interpretation, 36 to 45; the king's response, 46 to 49. The hymn of verses 20 to 23 sits at the exact hinge of the chapter. Everything before it is a problem no one can solve. Everything after it is the solution that God has given.

The dream is described in descending order of value and ascending order of hardness: gold, silver, bronze, iron, and then iron mixed with clay. The detail that the metals grow cheaper while growing stronger in the legs, and then collapse in the feet, is a literary picture of power that hardens and becomes brittle. The interpretation reuses the same order in verses 37 to 43, so a listener can follow each metal to its kingdom.

The chapter's frame repeats. The chapter begins with the king's sleepless spirit and ends with a king on his face before a prisoner of war. In between, the phrase 'what will happen' in verses 28 and 29, which in Aramaic points to the future, keeps the focus on God's plan for history rather than Nebuchadnezzar's own fate.
context.historical:
Dream interpretation was a profession in Mesopotamia. Babylonian scholars kept written collections of omens, including dream omens, and the court employed trained experts who matched what a king saw to a catalogue of outcomes. The astrologers' complaint in verses 10 and 11 shows how they understood their craft. They could interpret a dream someone told them. To recover the dream itself would require the gods, 'whose dwelling is not with mortals.' Nebuchadnezzar's demand tests exactly that claim. Whatever the king's motive, whether suspicion that they would invent a convenient meaning or fear of an omen about his own dynasty, the demand strips the experts of their cover.

Verse 1 dates the dream to the second year of the reign, which sits oddly beside the three years of training in Daniel 1:5. The usual explanation is that Babylonian dating counted the king's accession year separately, so that Daniel's training ended within what the book counts as the second year. The text does not stop to explain, and a reader should simply know that the tension is real and has a reasonable answer.

The empires of the dream correspond to a historical sequence. Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC, and Persia fell to Alexander of Macedon in the 330s. After Alexander's death his realm was divided among his generals, and the Ptolemies in Egypt and the Seleucids in Syria intermarried and fought for generations. Daniel 11:6 and 11:17 describe such marriage alliances, and the footnote to 2:43 notes that the mixing is literally of 'the seed of men.' Whether the iron kingdom is Greece or Rome is a question the text invites without settling, and both views of it appear in the debate below.

Daniel's rise in verses 48 and 49 is also historical in scale. He becomes ruler over the province of Babylon and head of its wise men, a position at the top of the very guild that had just been condemned, and he secures positions for his three friends. The court that sought to destroy him ends by depending on him.
context.canonical:
Daniel 2 has a long ancestry in Scripture. The Old Testament has already told of two other servants of God who interpret a pagan king's dream by refusing credit for it. Joseph says, 'Don't interpretations belong to God?' Genesis 40:8, and 'I myself cannot do it, but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer,' Genesis 41:16. Daniel says the same, 'not because I have more wisdom than any man alive,' Daniel 2:30. The prophets also taught that God shames the wise of the nations. Isaiah 44:25 says He 'foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners,' and Isaiah 47:12-13 mocks Babylon's astrologers in nearly the scene of Daniel 2.

Most important, the chapter reuses the great promises of a kingdom. A stone becoming a mountain draws on Zion, 'the mountain of the house of the LORD' that will be raised above the hills, Isaiah 2:2, and on Psalm 2, where God installs His King on His holy mountain and says to Him, 'You will shatter them like pottery,' verses 6 to 9. Hosea 13:3 and Psalm 1:4 had already used the image of chaff blown from a threshing floor. And a kingdom that 'will never be destroyed' answers the promise to David of a throne established 'forever,' 2 Samuel 7:13.

Within Daniel the dream is reworked in chapter 7, where the same four kingdoms appear as beasts, but where one 'like the Son of Man' receives an everlasting dominion, Daniel 7:13-14. The New Testament quotes and alludes to the passage constantly. Jesus applies the stone imagery to Himself, Matthew 21:42-44 and Luke 20:17-18, and Acts 4:11 repeats it. The first words of Revelation, 'what must soon come to pass,' Revelation 1:1, echo the phrase of Daniel 2:28-29 in the Greek version, and Revelation 11:15 announces that 'the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author is writing, in the language of the empire, to people who have just watched their own nation reduced to a province. His main intention is to move the question of who rules from Babylon to God. Nebuchadnezzar is told that his greatness has been given to him, 'the God of heaven has given sovereignty, power, strength, and glory,' verse 37, so the king is introduced as a steward and not an owner. Daniel's own confession in verses 20 to 22, that God 'removes kings and establishes them,' is meant to be the lens through which the exiles read every news report from the palace.

The author also wants his readers to see how a believer lives in a court that is hostile to God. Daniel is courteous to Arioch, asks the king for time rather than demanding it, brings his friends into prayer before he acts, thanks God before he speaks to the king, and then deflects credit in verse 30. He intercedes for the very wise men who had mocked his faith, verse 24. This is the posture of someone who knows that revelation is a gift and not a possession.

Finally, the author means the stone to function as a comfort and a warning. For exiles it is the promise that no empire, including the one that is holding them, is permanent. For kings it is a warning that their glory is borrowed. The details of the metals are given to establish that God knows the future in detail, and to show that the whole sequence is moving toward one end.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a dream, an interpretation and a king's reaction. It is not a set of instructions about how Christians should regard governments or a timetable for prophetic events. Nebuchadnezzar's falling on his face and ordering incense in verse 46 is recorded without approval; Daniel does not rebuke him there, but the book will go on to show how fragile the king's grasp of the truth is, chapters 3 and 4. A reader should not conclude from this verse that believers may accept worship.

What does carry forward is the pattern. God's people are to pray together over impossible situations, as Daniel and his friends did in verses 17 and 18, to answer power with discretion, to refuse credit for what God has given, and to intercede even for adversaries. As for the content of the dream, the right use is the one the author intended: to take courage that history is under God's rule and ends with His kingdom, while resisting the temptation to turn the metals and toes into a code for newspaper headlines. The text itself gives only a short list of kingdoms and does not hand us a calendar.

debates.question: Which kingdoms do the four metals represent, and especially the fourth?

views.label: Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece, Rome
views.case: The head of gold is named as Babylon, verse 38. Daniel 8:20-21 later names Media and Persia together as a single ram and Greece as the goat, so the silver and bronze fit Persia and Greece. The iron that crushes everything fits Rome, and the later weakness and mixing of the feet fits Rome's division. Because the stone comes 'in the days of those kings,' verse 44, this view places Christ's first coming in the days of the Roman Empire. It is the reading of most of the church from the early centuries.

views.label: Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece
views.case: Daniel 8:20 treats Media and Persia as one, but Daniel 5:28 and 6:8 speak of the Medes and Persians in a way that some read as two stages, and Darius the Mede reigns before Cyrus. On this view the bronze is Persia and the iron is Greece, whose generals' successor kingdoms, the Ptolemies and Seleucids, intermarried without uniting, verse 43. The little horn of Daniel 7 and Daniel 8 is read as Antiochus IV.

views.label: Rome revived
views.case: Some take the iron and clay feet and the toes as a future ten kingdom form of the fourth empire, to be crushed by Christ at His return. They link verse 41 with the ten horns of Daniel 7:24 and Revelation 17:12-14.

debates.bearing: The text names only the head of gold. It spends far more words on the stone than on the metals. All three views hold that the sequence ends in a kingdom no human hand produces and that it will last forever. Hold the identifications as proposals, and hold the stone as certain.

debates.question: When does the stone strike, and what is its kingdom?

views.label: At Christ's first coming and ever since
views.case: Verse 44 says the kingdom is set up 'in the days of those kings,' and Jesus announces that 'the kingdom of God is near,' Mark 1:15. It begins small like a mustard seed and grows, Matthew 13:31-33, and Jesus says of Himself that the one who falls on this stone will be broken and the one on whom it falls will be crushed, Matthew 21:44. The stone is at work now, and will be consummated at the end.

views.label: At Christ's return
views.case: The stone strikes the feet in a sudden blow and the whole statue is destroyed at once, verse 35, which suits Christ's final coming in judgment better than the quiet growth of the church. Earthly empires have not yet been 'shattered,' and the mountain has not yet filled the earth. Revelation 11:15 places the kingdom of the world becoming the Lord's at the last trumpet.

views.label: In the Maccabean age
views.case: Critical readers who date the book to the second century see the stone as God's coming rescue from the Hellenistic kings, in the days of the Seleucids, without reference to the New Testament.

debates.bearing: The New Testament holds both tenses together: the kingdom has come and is not yet consummated, 1 Corinthians 15:24-25. The first stroke fell at the cross and resurrection, and the final stroke is still ahead. Whichever timing a reader prefers, the stone's source is God and its end is the whole earth.

study.originalLanguages:
The Aramaic of this chapter is full of vocabulary that was chosen with care, and five items are worth setting beside the words the study has already highlighted.

First is the phrase in verse 28, be'achariyth yomayya, 'in the latter days.' The Hebrew counterpart appears in Genesis 49:1, where Jacob tells his sons what will befall them 'in the days to come,' in Numbers 24:14, and in the prophets, for example Isaiah 2:2, 'in the last days.' It names the stretch of time in which God brings His purposes to completion, and by using it Daniel says that the dream is not about Nebuchadnezzar's next war but about the shape of the whole of history under God. The Greek version translates it in a way that Revelation 1:1 echoes, 'what must soon come to pass.'

Second is peshar, 'interpretation,' which the chapter uses again and again, verses 4 to 9, 16, 24 to 26, 30, 36 and 45. It carries the sense of a solution or loosening, the untying of a knot. The Dead Sea community later used the same word for the genre of commentary in which a prophecy is said to apply to their own times. In Daniel the word is more modest. It is a gift of God that explains what He has already shown, and Daniel never claims to produce it himself.

Third is gelah, to reveal or uncover. God is gali raziyya, the 'Revealer of Mysteries,' in verse 47, and in verse 22 He 'reveals the deep and hidden things.' The picture is of something covered being uncovered, and it carries a prophetic note, since Amos 3:7 says God 'does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets.' The chapter makes Daniel a prophet in the older sense, one to whom God discloses what He is doing.

Fourth, the hymn of verse 21 says God 'changes the times and seasons,' using the Aramaic words iddan and zeman. The first of these returns in chapter 4, where the king is sentenced until 'seven times pass him by,' and the same word is used there. The hymn is therefore a promise whose fulfilment will be shown in the next story, in which the God who changes times is the God who sets the length of a king's humbling.

Fifth, the stone is 'cut out,' not by human hands, verses 34 and 45, using a verb for cutting as a mason cuts rock, in a form that does not name who does the cutting. The Aramaic for 'not by human hands' is a negative with the word for hands. Daniel 8:25 uses a Hebrew idiom of the same sort, 'broken off, but not by human hands,' for the end of a king, and the Bible reserves the language of hands for idols and for man's efforts. The footnote at verse 34 notes that the Greek version has the stone cut out 'from a mountain,' and verse 45 says that it was cut 'out of the mountain,' so the origin of the stone is the divine mountain, the place of God's rule, rather than any human quarry.

typology.type: The stone cut without human hands
typology.fulfillment: The stone is a kingdom made by God without human work. It corresponds to the rejected stone of Psalm 118:22 and the tested cornerstone laid in Zion, Isaiah 28:16, and Jesus takes both to Himself, Matthew 21:42-44, and so does Peter, 1 Peter 2:4-8. The escalation is that the stone is a person who is crushed in order to bring in the kingdom, and then raised. The correspondence breaks down at one point: the stone in the dream only destroys, while Christ also saves, so that 'the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.'

typology.type: The stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth
typology.fulfillment: A small thing grows until it fills everything. Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed and like leaven, Matthew 13:31-33, and the prophets had said that 'the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea,' Habakkuk 2:14. This growth is realized in the church's mission to all nations, Matthew 24:14 and 28:18-20, and its end is the new creation where the holy city comes down, Revelation 21:2-3. The dream only pictures the growth; the New Testament shows its means, the gospel.

typology.type: The image of gold and iron, fallen kingdoms
typology.fulfillment: The statue is the proud image of human power and in some ways recalls an idol, which Daniel 3 will turn into a golden statue that the king demands to be worshipped. Its fall corresponds to the destruction of every worldly claim to ultimate authority, which Christ will bring when He 'has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power,' 1 Corinthians 15:24. It falls short as a type only in that it is an image and not a person: it shows what falls, and Christ is the one who stands.

The secret that no wise man could recover and God gave to Daniel anticipates the larger mystery of Christ, 'hidden for ages and generations but now revealed,' Colossians 1:26, and 'the mystery of Christ' by which Gentiles become fellow heirs, Ephesians 3:4-6. Daniel was shown the shape of the future; the apostles saw its centre. The pattern is that God reveals through chosen servants what no human search can find, and the fulfilment is that the secret is now a person who can be known.

study.christ:
The strongest line from Daniel 2 to Christ is the stone, and Jesus Himself draws it. In Matthew 21:42-44 He quotes Psalm 118 about the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone, and He then adds a sentence that is almost a quotation of Daniel 2: 'He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.' Luke 20:17-18 records the same. Jesus is saying that He is the stone of Daniel's dream, and that every kingdom and every person must come to terms with Him. Peter takes up the same chain of stones in Acts 4:11-12 and 1 Peter 2:4-8, calling Christ 'the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God's sight.'

The kingdom of the dream is also the kingdom Jesus proclaims. When He says 'the kingdom of God is near,' Mark 1:15, He is announcing what Daniel's God said He would set up. The angel's promise to Mary uses the language of the chapter, 'His kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:33, and echoes the line that this kingdom 'will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people.' Jesus' own parables of the mustard seed and the leaven, Matthew 13:31-33, answer the question of how a kingdom that starts small can fill the earth.

The title the book gives Nebuchadnezzar, 'king of kings,' verse 37, is a title that the New Testament takes from him and gives to Christ. Revelation 19:16 writes 'KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS' on His robe, and 1 Timothy 6:15 calls God the 'King of kings and Lord of lords.' Nebuchadnezzar held the title on loan, and Jesus holds it by right. The authority that was given to the head of gold is given in full to the risen Lord, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18.

The chapter also leads to Christ through its revelation. Paul calls the gospel the mystery 'concealed for ages past but now revealed,' Romans 16:25-26, and says that in Christ are the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3. Daniel could tell a king what would happen; the apostles proclaim the person at the centre of it. And Daniel's night of prayer with his three friends is a small picture of the church praying together for the mercy of God.

Care is needed in two places. The stone is not a code for any single event, and the New Testament holds the arrival and the consummation of the kingdom together. And Daniel himself is not the Christ figure of this chapter; he is explicitly the one who says that he has no wisdom of his own, verse 30, which sends every reader past him to the God who reveals.
study.god:
The central statement about God in this chapter is the hymn of verses 20 to 23, which is the longest piece of praise in the opening half of the book and is spoken before Daniel has any proof that the revelation will be believed. It teaches that wisdom and power belong to God, that He controls both time and rulership, that He gives wisdom to the wise, and that nothing is hidden from Him. These are claims about the doctrine of God, and they are claims about omniscience and sovereignty held together: He knows what lies in darkness, and He directs what happens in the light.

The chapter also shows that God's sovereignty is exercised through gift. The statue's head is gold because 'the God of heaven has given' Nebuchadnezzar sovereignty, power, strength and glory, verse 37, and He has given 'the sons of men or beasts of the field or birds of the air' into his hand, verse 38. That language deliberately echoes the original human commission in Genesis 1:28. The king's authority is a derived and temporary stewardship. Paul says the same of every government, 'there is no authority except that which is from God,' Romans 13:1, and Jeremiah says that God gave the lands to Nebuchadnezzar, 'My servant,' Jeremiah 27:6.

God is also seen as personal. He is 'the God of my fathers,' verse 23, a God with a history and with promises, and He responds to the prayers of four exiles who 'plead for mercy,' verse 18. The one who sets up and removes kings is the same God who hears a small group meeting in a house at night. The great and the near are not rivals in His character.

The chapter also holds together revelation and mystery. God is the Revealer of Mysteries, but the revelation is partial, and the stone and the mountain still await their fulfilment. He is not trapped by the king's demands and does not hand His secrets to the experts who claim a right to them. He gives them to a man who asks with humility, and He gives them so that a king might know.

For worship, the chapter gives a pattern. Daniel blesses God before he gets his answer to the king, and he blesses Him for the sake of the wise men who had not asked. The praise is addressed to God for who He is and for what He has done, and then it is turned toward the work of rescue. A church that worships a God who knows the end of history can face the news without fear and can pray for the very people who have threatened it.

crossReferences.note: The same four kingdoms returned as beasts, ending with the Ancient of Days and one like the Son of Man receiving an everlasting dominion. Chapter 2 sees the kingdoms from the king's side, as a splendid statue. Chapter 7 sees them from heaven's side, as ravenous beasts, and the two views together give the full picture.

Joseph tells Pharaoh that he cannot interpret dreams himself but that God will give a sound answer. Daniel's words in 2:30 follow the same pattern, which marks both as servants of God in a pagan court who refuse any credit for their gift.

God installs His King on His holy mountain and tells Him that He will shatter the rebellious nations like pottery. The stone that breaks the statue and the mountain it becomes are the same picture of God's own King defeating the kingdoms of the earth.

In the last days the mountain of the Lord's house will be raised above the hills, and all nations will come to it. The mountain that fills the earth in Daniel 2:35 shares this vocabulary, so that the stone's growth is the rising of Zion to rule the world.

Jesus quotes the rejected stone of Psalm 118 and adds that anyone who falls on this stone will be broken, and anyone it falls on will be crushed. In the Gospel setting He is identifying Himself with the stone of Daniel 2, and warning that no one can be neutral.

At the seventh trumpet loud voices announce that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and that He will reign forever. It is the fulfilment of Daniel 2:44 in the language of the last book of the Bible.

Christ hands over the kingdom to the Father after destroying every dominion, authority and power, reigning until all enemies are under His feet. Paul has the shape of the dream in view: every rival power is crushed and the one kingdom remains.

Babylon's sorcerers and astrologers cannot save her, however long she has trusted them. It is a prophecy of the very failure that Daniel 2:10-11 stages at the court, and it shows that the vanity of Babylon's wisdom was announced beforehand.

God says He gives the earth to whom He pleases and has placed these lands under Nebuchadnezzar His servant, until the time of his own land comes. This is the doctrine of Daniel 2:37-38 stated by a prophet, and it shows the kingdom's gold is borrowed gold.

Paul speaks of the mystery of Christ, hidden in earlier generations and now revealed by the Spirit, that Gentiles are fellow heirs. The Greek word is the one used for Daniel's mystery, and Paul presents the gospel as the final unveiling of what God has been disclosing since the exile.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 1 gave humanity dominion over the beasts of the field and the birds of the air, and Daniel 2:38 uses nearly the same list when it says that God has given these into the king's hand. That is the point of contact with the beginning. Humanity was meant to rule creation under God, and in Babylon we meet what that rule has become: a human empire, magnificent and fragile, that rules but cannot know the future and cannot make itself last. The statue is the whole project of Genesis 11, 'let us make a name for ourselves,' written large in gold and iron.

Against that, the book offers the oldest hope in the Bible, that God will establish a kingdom of His own. The promise to Abraham of blessing for all nations, the promise to David of a throne forever, the prophets' mountain of the house of the Lord raised above the hills, all stand behind the stone. Daniel 2 is the place in the Old Testament where that kingdom is set directly against the rise and fall of world empires and given a time, 'in the days of those kings,' verse 44.

The Gospels announce that the time has come. Jesus proclaims the kingdom, is rejected by the builders and raised, and sends His followers to every nation. The kingdom that began as a stone no one noticed is now a mountain whose gospel reaches the ends of the earth, and Paul can say that Christ must reign until every enemy is under His feet. The sequence of empires in the dream becomes, in Daniel 7 and Revelation 13 to 19, the background to the war between the beast and the Lamb, and the Lamb triumphs.

The story ends where the dream ends, with a fullness. Revelation 11:15 hears that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and of His Christ. Revelation 20:11, in a line that closely echoes the 'not a trace of them could be found' of Daniel 2:35, sees earth and heaven flee from the throne, and 'no place was found for them.' Then Revelation 21 sees a new heaven and a new earth and God dwelling with man. What Nebuchadnezzar glimpsed in a dream is the end of the story the Bible tells: every rival throne gone, the kingdom of the Most High filling the whole earth, and the exiles of every age at home.

quiz.q: What made the king's demand of his wise men impossible?

options.text: He required them to tell both the dream itself and its interpretation, which they said only the gods could do.
options.note: Daniel 2:5-11 shows the demand exposed the emptiness of Babylon's wisdom.

options.text: He asked them to interpret a dream he described in detail.
options.note: The impossible part was that he would not tell them the dream at all.

options.text: He demanded they build a golden statue overnight.
options.note: The statue was in the dream; the demand was to recover and interpret the dream.

options.text: He asked them to predict the weather.
options.note: The demand concerned the forgotten dream and its meaning, not weather.

quiz.q: How did Daniel come to know the dream and its meaning?

options.text: The God of heaven revealed the mystery after Daniel and his friends pleaded for mercy in prayer.
options.note: Daniel 2:17-23 credits God, who reveals mysteries, in answer to prayer.

options.text: Daniel worked it out through superior training and intellect.
options.note: Daniel explicitly denies this in verse 30; the revelation came from God.

options.text: He bribed one of the king's servants for the secret.
options.note: There is no bribe; God revealed the mystery in a night vision.

options.text: He guessed based on the king's mood.
options.note: It was a direct revelation from the God of heaven, not a guess.

quiz.q: What does the statue of gold, silver, bronze, and iron represent?

options.text: A succession of human empires that rise in sequence and each pass away.
options.note: Daniel 2:36-43 interprets the metals as kingdoms following one another.

options.text: Four gods worshiped in Babylon.
options.note: The metals picture kingdoms, not gods, though Babylon was idolatrous.

options.text: Four seasons of the year.
options.note: The imagery is political, a chain of empires, not the seasons.

options.text: Four rivers of Babylon.
options.note: The metals stand for successive kingdoms, not rivers.

quiz.q: What does the stone cut without human hands represent?

options.text: The everlasting kingdom God Himself sets up, which shatters the empires and fills the earth.
options.note: Daniel 2:44-45 names it the kingdom that will never be destroyed.

options.text: A powerful new empire that will conquer by military force.
options.note: It is a kingdom, but one established by God, not by human power or armies.

options.text: A meteor striking the earth.
options.note: The stone is a symbol of God's kingdom, not a literal falling rock.

options.text: The city of Babylon itself.
options.note: The stone destroys the empires, including Babylon; it is God's kingdom.

quiz.q: How does the everlasting stone kingdom point to Christ?

options.text: Jesus brings the kingdom of God, and He is the rejected stone become the cornerstone whose reign fills the earth and never ends.
options.note: The New Testament ties the stone and the eternal kingdom to Christ, 1 Peter 2 and Mark 1:15.

options.text: It shows that God will one day set up some kingdom, with no link to Jesus.
options.note: The kingdom is real and future-facing, but the New Testament identifies it with Christ.

options.text: It predicts a Christian political empire that rules by force.
options.note: The kingdom comes not by human hands but by God's own act in Christ.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ.
options.note: Christ is the stone and the King of the everlasting kingdom in the New Testament.

questions: Nebuchadnezzar could not sleep for fear of the future. Where are your own anxieties about what is coming, and how does it help to know the God of heaven already holds the future?
Daniel turned first to prayer with his friends before he acted. When you face an impossible situation, is prayer your first move or your last resort?
Daniel refused to take credit, insisting the revelation came from God alone. Where are you tempted to claim credit that belongs to God?
Every gleaming empire in the dream ended as chaff blown away. How does the passing nature of worldly power reshape what you give your life to?
The stone kingdom will fill the whole earth and never end. How does belonging to that unshakable kingdom steady you when the powers of this age feel overwhelming?

translationNotes.note: A footnote in the source marks that from this point, Daniel 2:4b through 7:28, the original text is Aramaic, the common language of the empire; the shift suits a section addressed to the Gentile world.
Statue may also be rendered image; the same word runs through the rest of the chapter for the great figure the king saw.
Cut out without human hands stresses that the kingdom comes by God's act, not human effort; the Septuagint adds that the stone was cut from a mountain.
The peoples renders an Aramaic phrase, literally the seed of men, describing alliances that fail to hold, like iron that will not bond to clay.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Daniel 2:1-49. Poetic lines in verses 20 to 23 rendered as flowing prose. Daniel 2:4b onward is Aramaic, so the load-bearing lexicon entries use Aramaic.
